Compare the resulting fraction (not the percentage) against cap_fraction to decide whether the budget is breached.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The function separates total hours (all tasks) from toil hours (only tasks flagged is_toil) and divides to get the fraction actually spent on toil -- 10 toil hours (3 + 2 + 5) out of 20 total hours, exactly 50%. Because the breach check uses strict greater-than against the cap fraction, exactly 50% does not count as breached in this implementation -- a deliberate, defensible choice worth noticing, since a stricter policy might use `>=` instead; either is reasonable, but the function needs to pick one explicitly rather than leave the boundary ambiguous. The empty-list guard avoids a crash on a week with no logged tasks, returning a sensible default rather than raising a ZeroDivisionError.

exercises.prompt: A team decided a recurring manual task -- resetting a stuck queue by hand -- was toil, and immediately built an elaborate automation system for it, spending two full engineer-weeks. It turned out the task only occurs about once every four months and takes ten minutes each time. Identify the flawed reasoning and describe what should have happened instead.
exercises.code:
Decision log: "This task is manual and repetitive, so by definition it's toil, and
toil should be automated. Approved: two engineer-weeks for a full automated
self-healing system for the queue."
hints: The team correctly identified the task as toil using the definition -- the flaw isn't in that classification, it's in what they concluded should happen next.
Compare the actual cost of the manual toil over a year (frequency x time per instance) against the cost of the automation that was built.
The right question isn't 'is this toil, yes or no' alone -- it's 'does the frequency and cost of this specific toil justify this specific automation investment right now.'
exercises.solutionCode:
Corrected reasoning: This task is toil by definition (manual, repetitive,
automatable, no enduring value). However, at roughly 3 occurrences a year and
10 minutes each, it costs about 30 minutes of engineer time annually --
negligible compared to the two engineer-weeks (roughly 80 hours) spent building
an elaborate automated system for it. The correct decision at this frequency
and scale is to tolerate the manual toil for now, and revisit automating it only
if frequency or per-instance cost increases significantly as the system grows.
A five-minute script wrapping the existing manual steps (rather than a full
self-healing system) would likely have been the more proportionate response even
if some automation was still desired.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The team's classification of the task as toil was correct, but toil classification alone doesn't answer whether automation is worth building right now -- that requires comparing the actual cost of the toil (frequency times time per instance) against the cost of the automation investment. At roughly 30 minutes of manual cost per year against roughly 80 hours of engineering investment, this was a wildly disproportionate response; automating this specific toil would likely never pay back its own build cost, let alone the ongoing cost of maintaining it. This illustrates the misconception directly: not all toil should be automated immediately just because it's correctly labeled toil -- the automate-vs-tolerate decision needs its own evaluation based on real frequency and scale, and skipping that evaluation leads to exactly this kind of expensive overcorrection.

assessments.prompt: A team's on-call engineer spends significant time each week manually deciding which of several plausible root causes explains a new, previously-unseen failure pattern in a complex service interaction -- each instance is different and requires weighing ambiguous evidence. According to the definition of toil used in this concept, is this toil?
options: Yes, because it's manual and takes real time each week.

No, because it requires genuine judgment to weigh ambiguous, differing evidence each time -- it isn't automatable in the way the definition requires, and diagnosing it correctly leaves behind durable knowledge, unlike toil.
Yes, because any work that could theoretically be reduced with better tooling counts as toil by definition.
It depends only on how many hours per week it consumes, regardless of what the work actually involves.
assessments.explanation: Toil's definition requires the work to be repetitive in a way that's automatable and to leave no enduring value once completed -- this scenario fails both tests: each instance genuinely differs and requires weighing ambiguous evidence (not a fixed set of steps a script could follow), and correctly diagnosing a novel failure typically produces durable knowledge about the system, unlike restarting a known-hung process for the fiftieth time. Option A wrongly uses 'manual and time-consuming' as the entire test, when the definition is more specific than that. Option C overextends the definition to include anything tooling could theoretically help with, which would make almost all engineering work count as toil, emptying the term of its usefulness. Option D ignores the nature of the work entirely in favor of raw hours, which is exactly the kind of oversimplification the precise definition exists to prevent.

assessments.prompt: A team's toil has grown steadily over several quarters as the number of servers they operate has tripled, while the team's headcount has stayed the same. According to this concept, why does this create a compounding, self-reinforcing problem rather than a simple, steady annoyance?
options: It doesn't actually compound -- toil grows linearly and predictably, so it's always straightforward to plan for well in advance.

A team increasingly consumed by toil has correspondingly less time available to build the automation or fix the root causes that would reduce that toil, so the toil keeps consuming a growing share of capacity precisely because nobody has the spare time left to address it.
The problem is entirely solved simply by hiring one additional engineer for every quarter that server count grows.
This is only a compounding problem if all of the added servers happen to run the exact same software version.
assessments.explanation: The concept names this exact dynamic a 'vicious flywheel': toil scales with what's operated while headcount typically doesn't, and a team too consumed by toil has no time left to automate it away, so toil keeps consuming an ever-larger share of capacity as the system keeps growing. Option A contradicts the concept's explicit description of a compounding, self-reinforcing relationship. Option C assumes a scaling fix the concept never guarantees works cleanly in real organizations, where headcount rarely grows to match. Option D introduces an irrelevant technical condition that has no bearing on the structural scaling mismatch described.

assessments.prompt: A manual task that takes five minutes to perform occurs only about twice a year. According to this concept's reasoning about the automate-vs-tolerate decision, what is the most defensible response?
options: Automate it immediately, since anything correctly classified as toil should always be automated as soon as it's identified.

It's very likely cheaper to simply keep doing the task manually for now, since the low frequency means the total annual cost is small, and the ongoing cost of building, testing, documenting, and maintaining automation would likely exceed the toil it eliminates -- though the decision is worth revisiting if frequency or scale changes.
Ignore it permanently and never revisit whether it should be automated, since it's already been correctly identified as low-priority.
Escalate it to leadership immediately as a reliability risk requiring a formal incident review.
assessments.explanation: The concept directly rejects the 'automate everything labeled toil immediately' instinct, giving almost this exact example: a task that's rare and low-cost is very likely cheaper to keep doing manually than to build and maintain automation for, though the decision should be revisited as frequency or scale changes. Option A restates the misconception this concept explicitly corrects. Option C ignores the concept's explicit point that the calculation should be revisited over time, not decided once and forgotten. Option D wildly overstates the significance of a rare, low-cost, five-minute task.

assessments.prompt: One team reports 20% toil this quarter after holding steady near that level for over a year. A second team also reports 20% toil this quarter, but was at 8% two quarters ago and has been climbing steadily since. According to this concept, how should these two teams' situations be assessed differently, despite the identical current reading?
options: They shouldn't be assessed differently at all -- the current percentage is the only number that matters, and both teams are equally healthy right now.

The second team is in a meaningfully less healthy position despite the identical snapshot, because the rising trend suggests toil is actively growing and will likely breach the cap soon if unaddressed, whereas the first team's stable trend suggests its toil is currently under control.
The first team should actually be more concerned, since a long period of stability suggests complacency about automation opportunities.
Neither team's trend matters at all unless one of them has already breached the 50% cap outright.
assessments.explanation: The concept makes this exact comparison explicit: a team steadily near 20% toil is in a fundamentally healthier position than one that was at 8% two quarters ago and has been climbing since, even though both might read a similar number on any single day checked in isolation -- tracking the trend matters as much as any single measurement. Option A ignores the concept's explicit point that trend, not just snapshot, determines health. Option C inverts the concept's actual concern, treating stability as a problem rather than a sign of control. Option D wrongly implies trend data is irrelevant until the cap is already breached, contradicting the concept's point about catching problems before they become a crisis.

assessments.prompt: Explain why toil is described as a structural risk that compounds over time, rather than simply a source of day-to-day annoyance, and describe the mechanism that lets a team catch a rising toil problem before it becomes a crisis.
assessments.modelAnswer: The structural danger in toil comes from a scaling mismatch: toil tends to grow with the number of things being operated -- more servers, more customers, more edge cases discovered as a system runs in production -- while a team's headcount typically doesn't grow at anywhere near that same rate, and often barely grows at all between planning cycles. If toil isn't actively managed, its share of the team's total capacity rises simply because the system it supports keeps growing, independent of anything the team is doing wrong day to day. This creates a genuinely compounding, self-reinforcing problem rather than a static annoyance: a team increasingly consumed by toil has correspondingly less time available to build the automation or fix the root causes that would reduce that toil, so the toil keeps consuming a growing share of capacity precisely because nobody has the spare time left to address it -- a flywheel that, left unaddressed, can end with a team spending nearly all its time just keeping the current system running, with essentially nothing left over for the engineering work that would actually improve it. The mechanism that catches this early mirrors the same idea behind an SRE error budget: set an explicit, pre-agreed cap on the fraction of time that should go to toil (a commonly cited reference point is around 50% for operations-heavy roles), and actually track real toil hours against that cap over time, not just as a single snapshot. Tracking the trend, not just a point-in-time number, is what matters -- a team steadily near 20% toil is in a fundamentally healthier position than one that was at 20% two quarters ago and has been climbing since, even though both might read a similar number if checked in isolation on any single day. When the tracked trend crosses the pre-agreed cap, that crossing is the trigger to pause other work and invest deliberately in automating the highest-volume sources of toil -- the same way exhausting an error budget triggers a pre-agreed shift toward reliability work -- rather than waiting for the problem to become obvious only once the team is already buried in it.
